Welcome—I'm so glad you're here with me. Together, we're about to step into a story that reveals just how strong the human spirit can be, even when faced with unthinkable horror.
Imagine a place where every single day is a test of courage and hope. That's exactly what Olga Lengyel brings us in her powerful memoir, Five Chimneys: A Woman Survivor's True Story of Auschwitz. Through her eyes, we'll walk through the daily life inside a Nazi concentration camp—where illusions are stripped away, and both cruelty and quiet acts of heroism stand out starkly.
As we journey through the barracks, endure endless roll calls, and feel the constant shadow of danger, you'll notice something remarkable—small acts of kindness and moments of defiance that shine through the darkness. Amid all the loss and chaos, Olga's memories remind us of the friendships she forged, the glimmers of hope she clung to, and the difficult choices she faced just to survive.
We're invited to reflect on what it means to bear witness, to carry the stories of those who didn't make it, and to honor the responsibility of remembrance. Together, let's explore this journey from unimaginable suffering toward the fragile promise of freedom—and discover the enduring power of memory and resilience.

Chapter Four: The Role of Women—Strength, Suffering, and Small Acts of Defiance
Picture this: behind barbed wire and under the watchful eyes of guards in their towers, women endured a set of challenges that were uniquely their own. Life in the camp was shaped by gender at every turn—from the exhausting jobs they were given, to the risks they faced just to get through each day.
Women were often left with the toughest, most thankless tasks. Imagine scrubbing filthy floors, shouldering heavy loads, or sorting through the personal belongings of people who’d never return. It was backbreaking, demoralizing work.
The living conditions? Overcrowded, dirty, and almost unbearable. Privacy was nonexistent. Illness ran rampant, and even a minor infection could be life-threatening. Yet, in this harsh reality, many women fought to hold on to their dignity. Some found scraps of cloth and fashioned them into headscarves. Others carefully washed their faces, using water as if it were liquid gold. These simple, daily rituals—can you imagine?—became tiny acts of resistance, little reminders of who they were before the camp.
Pregnancy and motherhood made things even more precarious. Pregnant women were especially vulnerable during selections—often marked as unfit for work, and sent to their deaths. Mothers who managed to keep their children close faced heartbreaking choices. How do you protect your child when everything around you is designed to tear families apart? Some risked everything to hide their children during inspections. Others were forced to stand by, helpless, as their children were taken away.
Despite it all, women found ways to lift each other up. Friendships formed quickly, sometimes sparked by a shared hometown or a familiar face. These bonds were more than just emotional support—they were a lifeline. Sharing a scrap of bread, offering a comforting word, or tending to someone who was sick—these small gestures made a world of difference in a place where trust was rare.
And even when hope seemed lost, women found ways to push back. Some slowed their work on purpose, subtly sabotaging production or damaging equipment. Others risked everything to smuggle a message or a bit of food to someone in need. These acts might’ve seemed invisible to the guards, but for the women, they were powerful reminders that the spirit to resist couldn’t be stamped out.
Medical care in the camp was, at best, a faint hope. The women who worked as nurses or assistants did what they could, improvising treatments and offering comfort to those in pain. Facing suffering on such a massive scale was overwhelming, but even here, many women found strength through caring for others.
There was also the ever-present threat of sexual violence. Some guards abused their power, preying on the most vulnerable. The fear of assault added yet another layer of trauma. Still, women looked out for each other—warning friends about dangerous guards, forming protective circles, even stepping in to help when they could.
Through every hardship, the resilience of women shone through. Their ability to endure, to support one another, and to find moments of hope in the darkest circumstances is a powerful testament to the human spirit. The camp was designed to break people, but for many women, simply surviving became its own quiet rebellion—a refusal to let cruelty and hatred define them.

Chapter 6. The Tides of War: Rumors, Hope, and the Shifting Winds of Fate.
As the seasons changed, so did the mood in the camp. Days blurred together, but sometimes, out of nowhere, a whisper would break the routine—rumors that the war was shifting, that the Allies were moving closer, maybe even that freedom was within reach.
These stories floated through the barracks like the faintest threads of hope. Some nights, just one rumor could light up the whole room with cautious optimism. Other times, the silence that followed when nothing changed made hope feel almost painful.
For most people, those rumors cut both ways. Imagine overhearing a guard muttering about Russian tanks getting close. That night, you’d probably lie wide awake, caught between wanting to believe and fearing what it would mean if it wasn’t true. Around you, people whispered: is it safer to hope, even if it leads to heartbreak? Or should you just brace yourself for disappointment? But when you’re desperate, even the smallest scrap of good news is something to hold onto. Hope, no matter how thin, is a kind of lifeline.
As the front lines shifted, camp routines grew unpredictable. The guards were edgier, snapping more easily. Sometimes, work assignments were canceled without warning. Food rations—already barely enough—shrunk even more as supplies ran short. Oddly, all this uncertainty was both terrifying and a little electrifying. After so much monotony, even the threat of change felt better than the endless sameness.
One day, a group of prisoners was told to march to a new part of camp. Picture the woman, now thin and hollow-eyed, gripping her friend’s arm as they trudged through mud and snow. Even the guards seemed jumpy, glancing back over their shoulders, as if they expected something to happen at any moment. The prisoners felt it too—something was shifting, but no one knew exactly what.
In times like these, the smallest kindness meant everything. Someone sharing a hidden stash of potato peels, insisting her friends eat first. Another risking punishment just to pass along a scrap of hopeful news from a sympathetic worker. These tiny acts didn’t just fill empty stomachs; they reminded everyone that, even in a world built on cruelty, compassion could still survive.
As the war crept closer, the camp’s machinery started to break down. Some guards deserted, others became even more brutal, desperate to keep control. The prisoners felt the end might be near. Some started planning escapes. Others just prayed to make it one more day.
The air was thick with anticipation—and dread. It was like everyone could sense that the world outside was changing, and their own futures hung in the balance.

Let’s step into Chapter seven: Liberation—Chaos, Relief, and the First Steps Toward Freedom.
You know, the day liberation finally arrived wasn’t anything like what people had pictured in their minds. There was no big celebration, no clear moment when the nightmare was suddenly over and freedom began. Instead, it was a day tangled up with confusion, disbelief, and waves of emotion that no one could have prepared for.
It all started with the distant crackle of gunfire—quiet at first, then growing louder as the hours dragged on. The guards, who’d always seemed so strict and threatening, suddenly looked panicked. Some started shouting orders, while others just disappeared without a trace. Meanwhile, the prisoners huddled together in the barracks, caught somewhere between hope and fear, unsure if it was really safe to believe that the end had come.
When the gates finally swung open, there wasn’t any ceremony. It was pure chaos. Soviet soldiers marched into the camp, their faces set and serious as they took in the devastation around them. The prisoners were too weak to celebrate; most just stared in shock. Some broke down in tears, others laughed out of sheer disbelief, and a few simply collapsed, overcome by relief. There was one woman—clutching her friend’s hand—who felt this strange wave of unreality. After so much pain, freedom almost didn’t seem possible.
The days that followed are a blur in memory. The liberators did what they could—handing out food and medicine, trying to help—but the needs were just overwhelming. Many prisoners were far too sick or malnourished to make a recovery. The woman watched as some of her friends, who’d survived so much, finally gave in to exhaustion and disease. It was heartbreaking—liberation had come, but for some, it had come just a little too late.
For those who did survive, those first steps toward freedom were cautious and filled with uncertainty. The world outside the camp felt like another planet, and the future seemed both hopeful and terrifying at the same time. Some people desperately searched for any news of loved ones, holding onto the hope that someone, somewhere, had made it through. Others wandered the camp in a daze, struggling to make sense of what had happened to them.
The woman—now free, but deeply changed—found it hard to imagine life beyond those fences. All the habits of survival she’d learned—hoarding food, mistrusting strangers, always bracing for the worst—were tough to let go of. But as the days went by, she started to notice small joys again. The taste of real bread. The warmth of sunlight on her face. The simple sound of birds singing. Each of these moments reminded her that, even with scars, life could begin again.

Chapter 8. Aftermath: Searching for Family, Rebuilding Identity, and Facing the World.
Freedom—it's what she'd waited for, but it came with challenges she never imagined. Suddenly, she was left standing in the ruins of her old life, trying to make sense of what was left. Like so many others, her first instinct was to search for family. She moved from camp to camp, hospital to hospital, her eyes darting over endless lists of survivors, hoping to spot a name she knew. Each day brought a new ache—news that a husband was gone, children missing, friends vanished without a trace.
But even in the middle of all that heartache, there were small sparks of hope. Picture this—one noisy afternoon in a crowded refugee center, she suddenly saw a familiar face. It was a childhood friend, someone she’d thought was lost forever. That reunion was a mix of tears and laughter, stories poured out between them—tales of suffering, but also survival. It was these moments, these rare connections, that helped her start piecing together who she was again.
Getting back into the world wasn’t simple. She felt like a stranger in her own country. The home she remembered was now someone else’s. The things she’d owned—gone. And the scars from the camp? They weren’t just on the outside. Haunted eyes, frail bodies, nightmares that just wouldn’t let go. And when she tried to fit back in, some people looked on with suspicion, others with cold indifference. Sure, there was kindness here and there, but sometimes she was met with disbelief, even hostility.
Reclaiming her identity took time—and it was painful. She kept asking herself, who was she before all this? A mother, a wife, someone with a career. Memories of her family—both the happy ones and the tragic—became a strange mix of comfort and pain. So, she leaned into small routines: cooking a meal, planting a few seeds in a garden, writing letters to distant relatives. Every little act was a step forward, proof that she was more than just a number, more than what had happened to her.
And yet, the weight of memory was always there. She felt this deep need to bear witness—to make sure the world knew what had happened. She shared her story with anyone willing to listen. Neighbors, officials, strangers walking by. Telling the truth became both her duty and her way to fight back, to honor those who hadn’t made it out.
Over time, she found a little peace. She built new relationships, found work, even let herself dream about the future. The old wounds? They never disappeared. But she learned to live with them, to carry her memories with a kind of quiet strength. The world had changed, and so had she. Still, her will to survive, to love, and to hope—that stayed with her.

Chapter 9: Bearing Witness—The Responsibility of Memory and the Power of Testimony
As the years went by, her story grew into something much bigger than just a personal account. It became a testament—a powerful reminder of how resilient the human spirit can be, and how crucial it is to bear witness. She knew that surviving wasn’t the end of her journey. With survival came a responsibility: to remember, to speak up, and to make sure the horrors of the past wouldn’t just fade away.
She started to write, pouring her memories onto paper, hoping others might understand. It wasn’t easy—writing forced her to relive moments of terror and unimaginable loss. But, in a strange way, it helped her heal. It let her make sense of things that seemed senseless, and even helped her find meaning in her suffering. Her words reached people who’d been through similar ordeals, building a community grounded in memory and mutual support.
Of course, sharing her story came with its own set of challenges. There were people who doubted her, unable—or maybe just unwilling—to believe that such cruelty could exist. Some questioned her choices, her actions, even her right to survive. But she faced those doubts with quiet determination, standing firm in her belief that the truth had to be told—even if it made people uncomfortable.
She spoke to students, to officials, to anyone open to listening. Every time she shared her story, she had to relive the pain, but she also revisited moments of courage and unexpected kindness that had helped her carry on. She reminded everyone that within each of us lies the capacity for both good and evil—and that the decisions we make really do matter.
By giving testimony, she discovered a new sense of purpose. She became a voice for those who couldn’t speak, a living reminder of what had been lost—and what could still be rebuilt. Her story didn’t just echo in the past; it inspired others in the present to speak up, to remember, and to take a stand against injustice wherever it showed up.

Chapter 10: Lessons of Survival—Resilience, Humanity, and the Enduring Need for Hope
When she looked back, she realized survival wasn’t just about being lucky, or even about sheer strength. It came down to resilience—the ability to adapt, to find some kind of meaning in the middle of suffering, and most of all, to hold onto hope, even when things felt impossibly dark.
The lessons she learned in the camp were harsh, there’s no denying that. But those experiences uncovered deep truths about what it means to be human—truths you simply can’t learn any other way.
What really stuck with her, even years later, were the small acts of kindness. Maybe it was a shared crust of bread, a gentle touch, or just a few whispered words of encouragement. Those moments, more than anything else, made survival possible. They were like little reminders that, even in a world built on cruelty, our humanity can still shine through.
She also realized just how vital community was. In the camp, being isolated was almost a death sentence; connection meant life. The friendships she formed and the alliances she built gave her the strength to keep going. And even after liberation, those bonds stayed with her, reminding her she was never alone.
But maybe the most important lesson was about hope. Even when everything seemed lost, just believing that life could be different—that the suffering would eventually end—gave her the will to fight on. Hope wasn’t some naive fantasy. It was a powerful force—a way to picture a future that went beyond the pain she felt right then.
As she began sharing her story, she urged others to hold onto hope, to cherish their own humanity, and to stand up against injustice wherever they found it. She understood that suffering would never disappear completely from the world. But she also believed that by remembering what happened, and by acting with compassion, we really could build a better future.
Her story—and the stories of so many others—became a legacy. A living reminder that, even when we’re faced with unimaginable cruelty, the human spirit can endure, can resist, and ultimately, can triumph.

As we wrap up, let's bring all these lessons together. Even in the darkest places, it's those small acts of kindness that keep hope alive. Survival isn't just about getting through—it's about resilience, adapting, and leaning on the support of people around us. When we witness suffering, it weighs on us, but it also gives us the chance to stand up, to remember, and to care. Healing might feel slow, and reclaiming your sense of self can take time, but it’s always possible. And remembering what’s come before? Well, that’s what helps us build a more compassionate and understanding future. The story of Five Chimneys isn’t just about hardship—it’s a powerful reminder of how strong and complex the human spirit really is. Through one woman’s eyes, we see ordinary people facing unthinkable cruelty, yet still finding ways to endure, to resist, and to care for each other. The truth is, the lessons from Auschwitz aren’t locked in the past. They echo every time we’re asked to choose between indifference and compassion. So, what can you take from this? Know that what you do matters. The smallest gesture—a kind word, a willingness to listen, the courage to speak out—these are how we honor those who came before us, and how we build a better future. Healing isn’t always easy, and some scars might never fade, but by remembering, by witnessing, and by holding onto hope, we keep the dream of a world filled with dignity and humanity alive. Let the memory of those who suffered guide your choices, and let their resilience inspire you to meet life with empathy and courage, wherever you find yourself.
